Although Ciyao is said to have five phonetic tones, namely, high (H), low (L), downstep (!H), rising (LH) and falling (HL) (Whiteley 1966:7), phonemically there just two: H(igh) and L(ow) (Hyman and Ngunga 1994, Meeussen 1971, Mtenje 1990, Mtenje and Odden 1993, Odden 1994, 1997, Whiteley 1966) ... There is no lexical tonal contrast on verb roots. In Ciyao, verb tone is assigned by the inflectional morphology (tense/aspect system). ... Unlike verb roots, in which there is no H and L contrast, in nouns there is H and L contrast.' sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title (Philippson 1991, the 542-page Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu). theses.fr marks it not accessible and it is absent from HAL, archive.org and Persée, but an open full-text PDF (text, 542 pp.) is linked from the author's DDL/CNRS CV page and was downloaded, saved and read: Yao (P21) is one of the ~20 '++' core languages, gets its own case study (ch.4 sec.2.4, pp.102-109), is typed '(a):7, (b):1' (7 noun-stem tone patterns, no verb-stem contrast, Tableau II p.78), is called 'une langue très tonale' (p.251), is placed at diachronic 'stade I' (tonal assimilation without neutralisation, p.487), and in the annex fiche (pp.506-507) is coded 'langue tonale' with the penultimate's status given only as a tone-realisation rule; p.483 states outright that the penultimate plays no important role in the purely tonal systems, 'faible en yao'. This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'tonal' coding and supplies the explicit modern negative on penultimate accent that the catalog's deciding source (Ngunga 1997, silent on stress) lacked; recommend adding Philippson 1991 pp.78, 483-484, 506-507 as a supporting citation (does not replace Ngunga 1997). A related 1998 Faits de Langues summary article (doi:10.3406/flang.1998.1225) was surfaced by Crossref but is behind Persée's altcha challenge; low priority since the thesis itself was read.fr, HAL, Crossref, archive.org and the DDL site.

new_statements.reading: A first-hand comparatist who lists Yao among his best-described core languages classifies Yao as a tone language (lexical tone contrast on nouns, none on verb stems; all four Common-Bantu patterns retained; Meeussen's rule post-lexical) and explicitly rates the penultimate's role as weak, limited to one tone-realisation rule — i.e. no demarcative penultimate accent and no word-stress rule. This is the only modern source found that addresses the stress/accent axis for Yao head-on rather than being silent on it; it confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and closes the gap B flagged (modern sources silent rather than negative on stress).

tone_statements.quote: In most Bantu languages the accent is always placed on the last syllable but one, but this is not the case in ChiYao, and it is impossible to frame any rule for the guidance of the student, except that it never falls on the last syllable. In some words the accent is so evenly distributed that the stress cannot be recognised as falling on any one particular syllable; in other instances the accent is marked, but it may fall on any syllable except the last. Sometimes the accent is postponed by the addition of a suffix, in other cases no change is made. [...] III. THE INFLECTION OF WORDS. A number of words, identical in form, differ in meaning according to the inflection of the voice with which they are spoken. Taking the sign (') as indicating a rising, and (`) as a falling inflection, we differentiate, for example: ngangá, beer; ngangà, a guinea fowl; chitetè, a grasshopper; chitetè, native cloth

sources.citation: Hetherwick, Alexander. 1902. A handbook of the Yao language. London: SPCK (archive.org ahandbookyaolan00hethgoog).
sources.quote: 'In Yao the accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable (majzeimba), more rarely on the antepenult (wangali, waichile), never on the final syllable. When a suffix is appended to a word, the accent sometimes shifts so as to be on the penult (kumpilikina, kumpilikanila); sometimes it remains on its original syllable (waiche, waichile). The addition of the enclitic syllables -je, -ga, always draws forward the accent.'
sources.locator: ch. 'Sounds and sound-modifications' sec. 2 'Accent', pp.4-5 (djvu lines 931-954); same text in Hetherwick 1889 Introductory handbook (introductoryhan00hethgoog lines 1026-1047)

sources.quote: In Yao the accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable (majúmba), more rarely on the antepenult (wángali, wáichile), never on the final syllable. When a suffix is appended to a word, the accent sometimes shifts so as to be on the penult (kumpilikána, kumpilikaníla); sometimes it remains on its original syllable (wáiche, wáichile). The addition of the enclitic syllables -je, -ga, always draws forward the accent (waichéje, watamága). The demonstrative and personal pronouns, when the vowel is elided, are looked upon as forming an enclitic to the word, and so serve to draw forward the accent. Thus we have nyúmba aji, but nyumbá 'ji; ngúti une, but nguti 'ne. Elision of a vowel or consonant always draws the accent to the syllable where the elision takes place.
sources.locator: Ch; I 'Sounds and Sound-Modifications', sec. 2 'Accent', printed pp. 4-5; verb note printed pp. 57-58
sources.note: Accent-only account, no mention of tone anywhere in the grammar (the word 'tone' occurs only in dictionary glosses such as 'to speak in low tones'). Rule as stated: accent usually penultimate, more rarely antepenultimate, never final; suffixation sometimes shifts it to the penult and sometimes leaves it in place; the enclitics -je and -ga and elided demonstrative/personal pronouns always draw the accent forward (rightward) onto the syllable before the enclitic; elision draws the accent to the elision site. tone.quote: p. 171: "St. gibt a. a. O. S. III an, daß der Akzent (Starkton) im Yao schwer festzustellen ist. Die Rede fließt sehr gleichmäßig dahin. Nur die vorletzte Silbe hat einen etwas stärkeren Nachdruck. Außerdem versichert St., daß vor 'Doppelkonsonanten' — ich denke, er meint ny, nd, mb — der Vokal etwas länger ist. Das letztere ist sicher richtig, ich habe z. B. notiert: kalanga 'braten', nyanya 9 'Perlhuhn', numba 9 'Haus', ... Die erstere Behauptung ist aber nicht immer richtig. Man hört allerdings: kula 'wachsen', li-kumi 'zehn', nguku 'das Huhn', mesi 'Wasser', njuji 'Biene', li-tala 'Weg', numba 'Haus', ma-kala 'Kohlen', mina 'auspressen', aber hier ist die vorletzte Silbe eben zugleich die Stammsilbe. Wo dies nicht der Fall ist, betont man die drittletzte. Z. B. sagula 'auswählen', manilila 'wissen', gumbala 'voll sein' mit Nebenton auf der vorletzten; adjimje 'er hat gestohlen', kalanga 'braten' mit Nebenton auf der vorletzten, songola 'zuspitzen'."
